# Behcet disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Vasculitis > Behcet disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/_t05T3)

---

## Summary

Behcet disease is a type of variable vessel <u>vasculitis</u> that most commonly affects young adults (20–40 years of age) from the Mediterranean region to eastern Asia. Patients typically present with recurrent, painful oral and/or genital <u>ulcerations</u>; <u>uveitis</u> and <u>erythema nodosum</u> are also common in patients with Behcet disease. Diagnosis is based on clinical features, but diagnostic studies (e.g., <u>Doppler ultrasound</u>, <u>MRA</u> head) are required to assess for <u>end-organ damage</u> and exclude differential diagnoses (e.g., <u>aphthous stomatitis</u>, <u>reactive arthritis</u>). Management is based on the affected organs and disease severity, but often involves <u>immunosuppressive agents</u> (e.g., <u>glucocorticoids</u>, <u>azathioprine</u>) and <u>colchicine</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Most commonly affects individuals from the Mediterranean region to eastern Asia, with the highest <u>prevalence</u> observed in Turkey and Japan  [[2]](/library/FzXgu00)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–40 years of age

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Possible autoimmune and infectious triggers (e.g., precipitating <u>HSV</u> or <u>parvovirus</u> infection) [[3]](/library/NTX-Ix)

* Strong HLA-B51 association

---

## Pathophysiology

* Autoimmune systemic <u>vasculitis</u> that can involve <u>arteries</u> and <u>veins</u> of all sizes

* Characterized by the deposition of <u>immune complexes</u>, <u>proliferation</u> of <u>CD4+ T cells</u>, and increased <u>cytokines</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Recurrent painful oral <u>aphthous ulcers</u> (95–100%)

* Typically the initial presenting symptom

* Usually last about 1–4 weeks

* Recurrent genital <u>ulcerations</u> (60–90%)

* Single or multiple <u>ulcers</u> that resemble oral <u>aphthous ulcers</u> and heal with scarring

* Most commonly affect the <u>vulva</u> and the <u>scrotum</u>

* Ocular disease (50–80%) 

* <u>Uveitis</u> (<u>iridocyclitis</u>, <u>chorioretinitis</u>), <u>keratitis</u>, and/or retinal <u>vasculitis</u>

* Typically bilateral

* More common and severe among men

* Usually occurs 2–3 years after the onset of oral and/or genital <u>ulcers</u>

* <u>Skin</u> lesions (35–85%)

* <u>Erythema nodosum</u>, <u>papulopustular</u> lesions, pyoderma gangrenosum, pseudofolliculitis, or acneiform eruptions

* Dermatographism: formation of <u>urticaria</u> after minor pressure is applied to the <u>skin</u>, likely mediated by local <u>histamine</u> release

* Positive pathergy skin test: the appearance of an <u>erythematous</u> <u>papule</u> or <u>pustule</u> 48 hours after a 5 mm <u>skin</u> prick with a 20-gauge needle (usually on the forearm)  [[6]](/library/ezXx700)[[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)

* <u>Arthritis</u> (30–70%)

* Non-erosive, non-deforming, asymmetric <u>monoarthritis</u> or <u>oligoarthritis</u>

* Usually affects the knees, ankles, hands, and/or wrists

* Gastrointestinal disease: abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>anorexia</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>lower GI bleeding</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* Vasculopathy 

* <u>Superficial thrombophlebitis</u>

* <u>Thrombosis</u> of large <u>veins</u> (e.g., <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>, <u>Budd-Chiari syndrome</u>)

* Arterial <u>thrombosis</u>

* <u>Aneurysms</u> (e.g., <u>pulmonary artery</u> <u>aneurysms</u>)

* Neuro-Behcet syndrome (5–10%)  [[8]](/library/m-aVBM)

* <u>Parenchymal</u> <u>CNS</u> disease: behavioral changes, <u>ataxia</u>, <u>hemiparesis</u>, sudden <u>hearing loss</u>

* Non-<u>parenchymal</u> <u>CNS</u> disease: <u>cerebral venous thrombosis</u>, <u>intracranial hypertension</u>





> [!NOTE]
> PATHERGY: Positive <u>pathergy test</u>, Aphthous oral <u>ulcers</u>, Thrombosis (arterial and venous), Hemoptysis (<u>pulmonary artery</u> <u>aneurysm</u>), Eye lesions (<u>uveitis</u>, retinal <u>vasculitis</u>), Recurrent Genital <u>ulcers</u>, Young at presentation (3<sup>rd</sup> decade)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[2]](/library/FzXgu00)[[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)




* Diagnosis is primarily clinical.

* Diagnostic criteria may be used to establish a diagnosis.

* Diagnostic studies may be required to assess for <u>end-organ damage</u> and to exclude differential diagnoses.





> [!TIP]
> Rule out other conditions before starting potentially unnecessary and harmful <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Neuro-Behcet syndrome, vascular disease (e.g., <u>pulmonary artery</u> <u>aneurysms</u>), and GI disease are the main causes of mortality in Behcet disease and should be promptly identified and treated. [[2]](/library/FzXgu00)[[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)




### Diagnostic criteria




| <br>International Study Group diagnostic criteria for Behcet disease  [[2]](/library/FzXgu00)[[9]](/library/z91rJQ0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mandatory criterion | <br>* Recurrent (i.e., ≥ 3 episodes within a 12-month period) oral <u>aphthous ulcers</u><br><br> |  |
| Additional criteria | <br><br>* Recurrent genital <u>ulceration</u><br><br>* Ocular manifestations (e.g., <u>uveitis</u>, retinal <u>vasculitis</u>)<br><br>* Cutaneous lesions<br><br>* Positive <u>pathergy test</u> after 24–48 hours  [[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)<br><br><br> |  |
| A diagnosis may be established in patients who fulfill the mandatory criterion PLUS ≥ 2 of the additional criteria. |  |  |





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/FzXgu00)[[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)




* <u>CBC</u>: <u>leukocytosis</u>

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: ↑ <u>ESR</u>, ↑ <u>CRP</u>

* <u>Serology</u>: <u>Autoantibodies</u> (e.g., <u>ANA</u>, <u>ANCA</u>, <u>rheumatoid factor</u>) are usually absent.

* Genetic studies: <u>HLA-B51</u> testing is not routinely recommended. [[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)[[10]](/library/AzXRv00)





### Imaging studies [[7]](/library/8_XOJ00)




Consider imaging studies based on suspected conditions.




* <u>Doppler ultrasound</u> extremities: <u>VTE</u> and/or arterial <u>aneurysms</u>

* <u>MRI</u> head (with contrast): acute or chronic <u>parenchymal</u> neuro-Behcet

* <u>MRA</u> head: nonparenchymal neuro-Behcet (e.g., <u>cerebral venous thrombosis</u>, <u>cerebral aneurysm</u>)

* CT and <u>CTA</u> chest or abdomen: large-<u>artery</u> <u>aneurysms</u> and/or <u>thrombosis</u> [[11]](/library/g-XF900)[[12]](/library/XY19n20)

* Endoscopic studies: GI involvement and to rule out alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>Crohn disease</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[4]](/library/igXJEx)[[12]](/library/XY19n20)[[13]](/library/Lhbwet)




* Nonsevere disease

* Consult a rheumatologist and other specialists as required.

* Choice of therapy is based on the type of lesions.

* Severe disease : Consult a specialist (e.g., <u>neurology</u>, ophthalmology, <u>surgery</u>) and start treatment early to prevent permanent damage. [[13]](/library/Lhbwet)





> [!WARNING]
> Up to one-third of patients with GI involvement require emergency <u>surgery</u> as a result of <u>GI perforation</u>, <u>major bleeding</u>, or obstruction. [[13]](/library/Lhbwet)




### Pharmacotherapy [[12]](/library/XY19n20)




* Ocular disease, <u>CNS</u> disease, and/or vasculopathy

* <u>Systemic glucocorticoids</u>

* <u>Glucocorticoid-sparing agents</u> (e.g., <u>azathioprine</u>, <u>infliximab</u>, <u>cyclosporine A</u>, <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>IFN-α</u>, <u>methotrexate</u>)

* Aggressive treatment is required for severe sight-threatening <u>uveitis</u>.

* Mucocutaneous lesions

* Topical <u>glucocorticoids</u>;  (e.g., <u>triamcinolone</u> DOSAGE) can accelerate the healing of oral and genital <u>ulcers</u>.

* Immunomodulatory agents

* Consider <u>colchicine</u> to prevent lesion recurrence.

* For <u>colchicine</u>-resistant lesions, consider:

* Adding apremilast

* Other immunomodulatory agents (e.g., <u>azathioprine</u>, <u>thalidomide</u>, <u>IFN-α</u>)

* <u>Arthritis</u>

* First line: <u>colchicine</u>

* Consider intraarticular <u>glucocorticoids</u> in acute <u>monoarthritis</u>.

* Consider other <u>immunosuppressive agents</u> (e.g., <u>IFN-α</u>, <u>TNF-α inhibitors</u>, or <u>infliximab</u>) in chronic or recurrent cases.





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with severe disease usually require aggressive management with a combination of high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u> and other <u>immunosuppressive agents</u>.




### <u>Supportive care</u>




* Start <u>pain management</u>.

* <u>Prevent complications of glucocorticoid therapy</u>.

* Monitor for <u>adverse effects of immunosuppressants</u>.

* Consider <u>pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis</u>.
